definition: Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three classic properties information security tries to protect. Network attacks are often sorted by which of them they break.
example: Eavesdropping breaks confidentiality, tampering breaks integrity and a DDoS attack breaks availability.

definition: The security property that only the intended parties can read some data. On a network it is provided by encryption, such as TLS, a VPN or WPA2/WPA3 on Wi-Fi.
example: A passive eavesdropper on café Wi-Fi attacks confidentiality.

definition: The security property that data cannot be changed without the change being detected. Network protocols provide it with a message authentication code or an authenticated-encryption tag, not with a plain checksum.
example: TLS rejects a record whose authentication tag does not verify, so an on-path attacker cannot silently alter it.

definition: The security property that a message really came from who it claims to come from. Spoofing and replay attacks target it; certificates, signatures and message authentication codes protect it.
The security property that a service stays usable by its legitimate users. Denial-of-service attacks target availability.
Reading network traffic you were not meant to see, without changing it. Because nothing is altered it is very hard to detect; encryption is the defence.
example: A laptop in monitor mode near a café access point can capture other customers’ Wi-Fi frames.

definition: Encrypting data while it travels over a network, as opposed to while it is stored. TLS, VPNs and WPA2/WPA3 are examples.
Sending IP packets with a forged source address. Replies go to the forged address, so it suits one-way attacks such as reflection DDoS rather than conversations; BCP 38 filtering blocks much of it.
Allowing or blocking devices by their MAC address. It is weak security because a MAC address is sent in clear and can easily be changed to copy an allowed one.

A local network built from switches, which forward each frame only towards the port where the destination MAC address was learned. Eavesdropping then needs tricks such as ARP spoofing or MAC flooding.
A complete Ethernet frame carried as the payload of a tunnel such as VXLAN; its 14-byte header counts against the underlay’s MTU.

A fake Wi-Fi access point that copies a real network’s name (SSID) to lure clients, putting the attacker in the middle. Clients that properly authenticate the network (WPA3-SAE, or 802.1X with server-certificate checks) resist it.

Capturing a valid message and sending it again later. The attacker does not need to read or change it; defences make each message usable once with nonces, sequence numbers or authenticated timestamps plus duplicate tracking.
example: Resending a captured, correctly signed "pay £50" message ten times.

definition: A "number used once": a value that must never repeat under the same key or in the same context. Nonces make messages fresh against replay, and stream ciphers need a unique nonce per message or the keystream repeats.
Evidence that a message is new rather than a replay, such as an unused nonce, a higher sequence number or a recent authenticated timestamp.
A network of compromised devices (bots) under an attacker’s control, often used to send DDoS traffic or spam.
example: Mirai (2016) was built from hacked cameras and home routers.

definition: Malware that in 2016 built a large botnet from IoT devices with default passwords, and was used in DDoS attacks including the one that disrupted the DNS provider Dyn.
A US managed-DNS provider (later bought by Oracle). The October 2016 Mirai attack on its DNS service made many customer websites hard to reach.
A DDoS attack that fills the victim’s network links with more traffic than they can carry, measured in bits per second. It has to be mitigated upstream, before the congested link.

A DoS attack that exhausts a stateful resource, such as a server’s half-open connection queue or a firewall’s connection table, usually measured in packets per second. A SYN flood is the classic example.
A DoS attack using requests that look legitimate but are expensive to serve, such as searches, logins or uncached pages, measured in requests per second.
A provider with very large network capacity that receives a victim’s traffic during an attack, filters out the attack traffic and forwards the rest.
example: Cloudflare, Akamai and AWS Shield offer scrubbing.

definition: A large CDN and security company offering DDoS scrubbing among other services.
Amazon Web Services’ managed DDoS protection service for resources hosted on AWS.
A hash computed together with a secret key, so only someone with the key can produce or check the value. HMAC is the usual construction.
A low-bandwidth application-layer DoS attack that opens many HTTP connections and sends headers very slowly, never finishing, so a thread-per-connection server runs out of workers.
A challenge, such as picking images, meant to be easy for humans but hard for automated clients; used to slow down bots and application-layer floods.
A long-established open-source web server. Its classic process- or thread-per-connection modes are vulnerable to Slowloris because each slow connection ties up a worker.
An open-source, event-driven load balancer and reverse proxy for TCP and HTTP.
A server that handles many connections with a few threads and an event loop, rather than one thread per connection, so idle or slow connections cost only a little memory.
One of a fixed pool of threads a server uses to handle requests. When all are busy, new requests wait or are refused.
A DDoS technique in which the attacker sends requests with the victim’s address forged as the source to third-party servers (reflectors), so their replies flood the victim.

A reflection attack over UDP using requests whose responses are much larger than the requests, multiplying the attacker’s bandwidth by the bandwidth amplification factor. UDP is used because it has no handshake to verify the source.
Bandwidth amplification factor: response bytes divided by request bytes for a reflected protocol. It is measured, not fixed, and depends on which bytes (payload or headers) are counted.
example: A 40-byte request triggering a 1,400-byte response has a payload BAF of 35.

definition: When one request produces many response packets, multiplying packets per second as well as bytes, which stresses routers and firewalls.
Simple Service Discovery Protocol: part of UPnP, used by home devices to announce themselves on UDP port 1900. Devices that answer it from the internet can be abused as amplifiers.
Character Generator Protocol: an old test service (port 19) that replies with a stream of characters. Exposed UDP chargen services are amplifiers.
A DNS resolver that answers queries from anyone on the internet. Open resolvers are abused as reflectors in amplification attacks and should be restricted to their own users.
Best Current Practice: an IETF document series for recommended operational practice. A BCP number stays fixed while the RFC behind it can be updated.

The IETF best practice (RFC 2827) that networks drop customer packets whose source address is outside the prefixes that customer is allowed to use, so spoofed packets never leave the attacker’s network.
The first QUIC packet type, carrying the TLS ClientHello. Clients must pad datagrams with Initial packets to at least 1,200 bytes, which limits amplification.
Terabits per second: 10^12 bits per second, or 1,000 Gbps. The largest reported DDoS attacks are measured in Tbps.
Terabyte: 10^12 bytes in decimal units, or one million megabytes.
example: A full 1 Gbps capture produces about 10.8 TB a day.

definition: Petabyte: 10^15 bytes in decimal units, or 1,000 terabytes.
The control information at the start of a packet: addresses, ports, lengths and flags. Every layer adds its own; on an IPv4 packet with no options the IP header is 20 bytes, and the UDP header 8.
How data is divided into packets, and the per-packet overhead (headers, framing, gaps) that adds on the wire.
Short for layer 2, the link layer: where Ethernet, Wi-Fi and VLANs move frames using MAC addresses.
The extra bytes and gaps the link layer adds around each packet (Ethernet header, checksum, preamble and inter-frame gap). They use link capacity but are not part of the IP packet.
Splitting a network into zones with controlled paths between them, so that compromising one machine or zone does not give an attacker access to everything.
example: Putting databases in a zone only the app servers can reach.

definition: A security model (NIST SP 800-207) in which network location alone grants no trust: each access to a resource is evaluated using the user’s and device’s identity and policy, and re-evaluated as risk changes.
One line of firewall policy: a match on fields such as protocol, addresses and ports, plus an action such as allow (accept) or deny (drop or reject).
A filter that judges each packet on its own headers, with no memory of earlier packets. It therefore needs explicit rules for reply traffic, such as ephemeral port ranges.
example: AWS network ACLs are stateless.

definition: Filtering that uses a connection table, so rules can match connection state and permit replies to allowed traffic without separate rules.
example: AWS security groups are stateful.

definition: A firewall that understands application protocols such as HTTP and can match on their content, for example blocking a request path. NGFWs and WAFs are examples.
Checking rules in order from the top and applying the first one that matches, ignoring the rest. Rule order then decides the outcome, so specific rules must sit above broad ones.
What a firewall does with traffic that matches no rule. It should normally be deny, so anything not explicitly allowed is blocked.
Amazon Web Services: Amazon’s cloud platform. Its network controls include security groups, network ACLs, VPC Flow Logs and NAT gateways.
AWS’s stateful virtual firewall attached to network interfaces. It has allow rules only, evaluated together, and can reference other security groups as sources.
example: "Allow port 5432 from members of sg-web."

definition: Network access control list: AWS’s stateless filter applied at a subnet boundary, with numbered allow and deny rules evaluated lowest number first. Return traffic needs explicit rules.
The block of IP addresses a network or customer is allowed to send from. BCP 38 filtering drops packets whose source address falls outside it.
The current Linux packet-filtering framework (successor to iptables). Rules live in tables and chains attached to kernel hooks such as input.
The older Linux firewall tool, largely superseded by nftables. It used separate commands for IPv4 (iptables) and IPv6 (ip6tables), so forgetting the second left IPv6 unfiltered.
In nftables or iptables, an ordered list of rules attached to a point in the kernel’s packet path; the input chain sees packets addressed to the host itself.
The state conntrack assigns to each packet’s flow, such as new, established, related or invalid. Firewall rules can match on it, for example to accept replies to permitted connections.
A firewall rule that can never take effect because an earlier rule already matches every packet it could match.
A list of what is explicitly permitted; everything else is denied.
Controlling which traffic may leave a network or host. It can obstruct malware command-and-control and data exfiltration.
The channel through which an attacker sends instructions to compromised machines and receives their data. Malware often contacts its command server at regular intervals (beaconing).
Unauthorised transfer of data out of a network by an attacker. Unusual outbound volumes in flow logs are a classic sign.
The memory where a stateful firewall, NAT or load balancer records each active flow. It is finite, so floods of new flows can fill it and cause new connections to be dropped.
Linux’s connection-tracking subsystem, which records flows so firewall rules can match their state. By default it keeps an idle established TCP entry for five days.
The ICMPv6-based protocol IPv6 hosts use to find each other’s link-layer addresses and their routers (via router advertisements). Firewalls must let it through or IPv6 breaks.
The IPv4 and IPv6 versions of ICMP, the Internet Control Message Protocol that carries network error and diagnostic messages such as "packet too big". Blocking all of it breaks path MTU discovery.
The ICMP error a router returns when a packet is larger than the next link’s MTU and cannot be fragmented (ICMPv4 type 3 code 4, ICMPv6 type 2). It drives path MTU discovery.
How long a firewall, NAT or load balancer keeps an entry for a flow with no traffic before forgetting it. After that, the connection silently breaks.
example: AWS NAT Gateway: 350 seconds.

definition: A managed cloud service that lets instances in private subnets make outbound connections using shared public addresses. It has a connection table with idle timeouts.
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud: AWS’s virtual-machine service. Each instance connects through network interfaces with security groups.
Next-generation firewall: a firewall that identifies the application, user and sometimes content of traffic, not just ports and addresses.
Web application firewall: sits in front of HTTP services and blocks malicious request patterns such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Short for SQL injection: smuggling SQL commands into an application through its inputs.
Ending a TLS connection at a proxy or load balancer, which decrypts the traffic and forwards it, possibly re-encrypted, to the backend.
A middlebox decrypting TLS by impersonating servers with certificates from its own CA that clients have been told to trust. It restores visibility but breaks pinning and adds a high-value target.
A self-signed CA certificate at the top of a chain, trusted because it is installed in the client’s trust store. Its private key is often kept offline.
The set of root certificates a browser, operating system or application trusts. Membership varies between stores.
A client accepting only a specific certificate, key or CA for a service rather than any trusted one. It defeats TLS interception, which is why interception breaks pinned apps.
A network with no internal boundaries, where every machine can reach every other. One compromised device can then probe everything.
An attacker moving from the first compromised machine to others inside the network, looking for valuable systems or credentials.
Heating, ventilation and air conditioning. In the Target breach, credentials of an HVAC contractor were reportedly the attackers’ way in.
A network zone that holds internet-facing services, separated by firewalls from both the internet and the internal network, so a compromised web server is still outside.
Internet of Things: network-connected devices such as cameras, sensors and smart plugs, which are often poorly secured and best isolated.
Segmentation down to individual workloads: each service may talk only to the specific services it needs, usually enforced on the host or by the hypervisor.
How much an attacker can reach, or a failure can affect, from one compromised machine or identity. Segmentation shrinks it.
The traditional security model: a hard perimeter with broad trust inside it. It fails once an attacker gets one foothold inside.

aliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology
definition: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which publishes widely used security standards and guidance, such as the SP 800 series.
NIST Special Publication 800-207 (2020), which defines zero trust architecture.
Multi-factor authentication: requiring two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus a phone prompt or hardware key, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
Giving each user or service only the access it needs for its task, and no more.
Data that systems report automatically about their activity and health, such as logs, metrics and device posture, used for monitoring and security decisions.
The security state of a device, such as whether it is company-managed, patched and encrypted, used as an input to access decisions in zero trust.
Google’s zero-trust implementation, described from 2014, in which employees reach internal apps through an internet-facing access proxy based on user and device identity rather than network location.
A proxy in front of applications that checks who the user is and what device they are on for each request before passing it through.
Infrastructure (often sidecar proxies) that handles service-to-service traffic: issuing workload certificates, applying mTLS, and enforcing authorisation policy.
Firewall rule sets growing to thousands of entries nobody dares remove, hiding mistakes and unneeded access.
A firewall rule allowing any source to any destination, often added "temporarily" and never removed, which defeats the firewall.
The network interface or port used to administer a device or system. It is high-value and should be reachable only from a restricted admin network.
Single sign-on: one login, at an identity provider, that gives access to many applications.
Short for load balancer: a device or service that spreads connections or requests across several backend servers.
Shorthand for authentication (proving who you are) and authorisation (deciding what you may do). A certificate gives authn; policy gives authz.

The 2013 compromise of the US retailer Target, in which around 40 million payment-card accounts were exposed. Investigations pointed to a path from a compromised HVAC vendor’s credentials into sensitive areas of a poorly segmented network.
Secure Sockets Layer: the predecessor of TLS. All versions are broken and prohibited; "SSL" is still used loosely to mean TLS.
Pre-shared key: a secret both sides already hold before the handshake. In TLS 1.3 it usually comes from an earlier session (resumption); in WPA2-Personal it is derived from the Wi-Fi passphrase.
Mutual TLS: TLS where the client also presents a certificate and proves it holds the private key, so both ends are authenticated. Common between services in zero-trust designs.
An algorithm for encrypting and decrypting data with a key, such as AES or ChaCha20.
A named combination of algorithms a TLS connection uses. In TLS 1.3 it names the AEAD cipher and hash, such as TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256; key exchange and signatures are negotiated separately.
An attack that decrypts CBC ciphertext by sending modified versions and watching whether the receiver reports, or takes different time over, bad padding.

aliases: Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption
definition: A 2014 padding-oracle attack on SSL 3.0’s CBC mode, made practical by forcing a downgrade to SSL 3.0.
An old TLS key exchange in which the client encrypts the session secret with the server’s RSA public key. It has no forward secrecy, so TLS 1.3 removed it.
The property that stealing a long-term key later does not decrypt sessions recorded earlier, because each session used temporary keys that were then erased.
example: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman in TLS 1.3 gives forward secrecy; TLS 1.2 RSA key transport does not.

definition: Static Diffie-Hellman reuses the same key pair for many connections, so stealing it later exposes recorded sessions; ephemeral DH uses a fresh key pair per connection and erases it, giving forward secrecy. TLS 1.3 removed static DH.
A key generated fresh for one connection or session and then deleted. Erasing it is what gives forward secrecy.
A once-popular stream cipher with statistical biases and weak key scheduling. It broke WEP and was banned from TLS (RFC 7465).
An old 128-bit hash function with easy-to-find collisions; unsafe for signatures and removed from TLS 1.3.
Two different inputs giving the same hash. If attackers can create them, they can forge signatures, as with MD5 and SHA-1.
Re-running a handshake inside an existing TLS 1.2 connection. It was complex and attacked (CVE-2009-3555), so TLS 1.3 removed it.
A TLS 1.3 server reply asking the client to retry with a key share for a group the server supports, costing an extra round trip.
The TLS 1.3 server message, already encrypted, carrying the rest of the server’s choices, such as the agreed ALPN protocol.
A TLS handshake message containing a signature, made with the certificate’s private key, over a hash of the handshake so far. It proves the sender holds the key now and binds it to this key exchange.
The last TLS handshake message from each side: a MAC over the whole transcript with a handshake-derived key. If anyone altered an earlier message, it fails.
A TLS 1.2 message announcing a switch to new keys. TLS 1.3 may send dummy copies only so the handshake looks like TLS 1.2 to middleboxes.
The TLS message in which a server asks the client to authenticate with a certificate, as in mTLS.
A side’s public Diffie-Hellman value for a particular group, sent in the TLS 1.3 ClientHello or ServerHello so both can compute the shared secret.
A value both sides of a key exchange end up knowing but an eavesdropper does not; session keys are derived from it.
The unit TLS sends data in: a short header plus an encrypted, authenticated payload.
The sequence of handshake messages exchanged so far. TLS hashes it and signs or MACs the hash, so any tampering with earlier messages is detected.
Forcing two parties to use an older or weaker protocol version or option than both support, so a known weakness can be exploited. TLS 1.3 and WPA3 both include defences, with limits.
example: Advertising a WPA2-only copy of a WPA3 network to capture a crackable handshake.

definition: A fixed value that a TLS 1.3-capable server puts in the last 8 bytes of its random value when it negotiates an older version: the ASCII bytes "DOWNGRD" followed by 01 for TLS 1.2 or 00 for TLS 1.1 and below. A TLS 1.3 client that sees it can detect a forced downgrade.
An opaque value a TLS server gives the client after a handshake, which the client presents later to resume with a PSK and skip the certificate exchange.
An HTTP status (RFC 8470) a server returns to refuse a request received as early data, asking the client to retry after the full handshake.
The property that doing an operation several times has the same effect as doing it once. Idempotent requests are safer to replay, but idempotence alone does not make early data safe.
A signed document binding a public key to names (such as a domain), issued by a certificate authority. Clients check the signature chain, names and dates before trusting the key.
Certificate authority: an organisation that signs certificates after checking the requester controls the names in them. Clients trust CAs whose roots are in their trust store.
A CA certificate between a root and a leaf. Roots sign intermediates, which sign everyday leaf certificates; servers must send their intermediates along with the leaf.
The certificate for the server (or client) itself, at the bottom of the chain, naming the hostname it is valid for.
A certificate for the same subject and key as an existing CA certificate but issued by a different CA, creating an alternative path to a root that older clients trust.
The sequence of certificates from a leaf through intermediates to a trusted root, each signed by the next. The client verifies every link.
Subject Alternative Name: the certificate extension listing the DNS names (or IP addresses) the certificate is valid for. Clients match the hostname against it.
An older certificate field holding a name; browsers now ignore it for hostname checks and use the SAN instead.
A certificate extension saying whether the certificate belongs to a CA that may sign other certificates.
A certificate extension limiting what the key may be used for, such as TLS server authentication.
Public, append-only logs of issued certificates, so domain owners and monitors can spot mis-issued certificates. Browsers require evidence that public certificates were logged.
Signed certificate timestamp: a CT log’s signed promise to include a certificate. Browsers check SCTs for publicly trusted certificates.
A CA issuing a certificate it should not have, for example for a domain whose owner did not ask for it.
Declaring a certificate invalid before it expires, for example because its private key leaked, via CRLs or OCSP. Clients’ checking behaviour varies.
Certificate revocation list: a signed list of revoked certificate serial numbers published by a CA.
Online Certificate Status Protocol: asking a CA’s responder about the status of one certificate. Direct queries reveal to the responder which sites you visit.
The server fetches a recent signed OCSP response for its own certificate and sends it in the handshake, so clients need not contact the CA.
Accepting a certificate when its revocation status cannot be retrieved. Convenient, but an attacker who blocks the check defeats it.
A certificate valid for days or weeks rather than a year, limiting how long a stolen key is useful without relying on revocation. Requires automated renewal.
example: Public TLS certificates are limited to 47 days from March 2029.

definition: A free, automated, non-profit CA that issues TLS certificates using the ACME protocol. It ended its OCSP service in 2025 in favour of CRLs.
The industry body of certificate authorities and browser makers that sets rules for publicly trusted TLS certificates, such as maximum lifetimes.
Automatic Certificate Management Environment (RFC 8555): the protocol clients use to prove domain control and obtain and renew certificates automatically.
Renewing and installing certificates by software, before expiry, without human steps. Needed as lifetimes shrink.
Public key infrastructure: the CAs, certificates, policies and software that bind public keys to identities. The Web PKI is the public one browsers use.
Authority Information Access: a certificate extension with URLs, such as where to download the issuer’s certificate; browsers may use it to fetch missing intermediates.
A widely used open-source TLS library and command-line tool. openssl s_client connects to a server and shows its certificate chain.
Hybrid Public Key Encryption (RFC 9180): encrypts a message to a recipient’s public key using a key exchange plus an AEAD cipher. ECH uses it to encrypt the inner ClientHello.
The ECH configuration published in DNS: the client-facing server’s public key, its public name and parameters.
The provider’s client-facing name that appears in the outer ClientHello when ECH is used, shared by many sites so it reveals little.
With ECH, the real ClientHello (inner, encrypted) is carried inside a visible ClientHello (outer) that names only the public name.
The group of possible sites (or users) an observer cannot tell apart. With ECH, it is the sites sharing one public name and configuration.
DNS queries sent inside TLS or HTTPS to a resolver, hiding names from the network path but not from the chosen resolver.
A certificate authority an organisation runs for itself, trusted only by its own clients and services, for example to issue mTLS certificates.
An open-source service mesh that can issue workload certificates and apply mTLS and authorisation policy between services.

aliases: Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone
definition: Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone: a standard for naming workloads (SPIFFE IDs) and issuing them short-lived certificates.
A name for a machine or service, such as www.example.com, which DNS turns into an IP address and TLS checks against the certificate.
Uniform Resource Locator (a kind of URI): a web address such as https://clinic.example/appointments. In HTTPS only the hostname leaks; the path is encrypted.
Settings (in Python requests and ssl) that turn certificate checking off, leaving TLS open to any man-in-the-middle.
The virtual network interface a tunnel or VPN creates on a host or router. Packets routed to it are encapsulated and sent to the far tunnel endpoint; its MTU must allow for the tunnel’s overhead.
Removing the outer tunnel headers at the far end of a tunnel to recover the original inner packet or frame.
A VPN that connects an individual device to an organisation’s network, putting it logically "on the network".
The device or service that terminates VPN tunnels for a network. Internet-facing, so a frequent target.
The extra bytes a tunnel or protocol adds to each packet, which reduce the space for the inner packet.
example: VXLAN over IPv4 adds 50 bytes.

definition: The physical network that carries tunnelled traffic between tunnel endpoints.
A virtual network built from tunnels over an underlay, such as VXLAN segments between hypervisors.

Path MTU discovery done by the transport protocol itself (RFC 8899 for datagrams, RFC 4821 for TCP): it probes with larger packets and watches what gets through, so it works even when ICMP Packet Too Big messages are blocked.
An IPv4 header flag telling routers not to fragment the packet but to drop it and report Packet Too Big. IPv6 routers never fragment.
A router or tunnel edge rewriting the maximum segment size in passing TCP SYNs to a smaller value, so endpoints never send segments too big for the tunnel. It does not help UDP.
A helper script that brings up a WireGuard interface from a config file, setting addresses, routes from AllowedIPs, and the MTU.
A suite of protocols that secures IP packets at the network layer: IKEv2 authenticates peers and agrees keys, and ESP (or AH) protects each packet.
Internet Key Exchange (version 2, RFC 7296): IPsec’s control protocol on UDP 500 (4500 with NAT). It authenticates the peers, negotiates algorithms and sets up security associations.
Security association: the agreed algorithms, keys and identifiers for one direction (or, for IKE, both directions) of protected traffic between two peers.
Security Parameters Index: a number in each ESP/AH packet header (and in IKE) telling the receiver which security association to use.
Encapsulating Security Payload (IP protocol 50): IPsec’s packet format that encrypts and/or authenticates packets, with an SPI and sequence number in its header.
Authentication Header (IP protocol 51): IPsec’s integrity-only format, which also covers unchanging IP-header fields, so it conflicts with NAT. Rarely used now.
An IPsec mode that protects the payload of an IP packet but keeps the original IP header, usually for host-to-host protection.
An IPsec mode that encrypts the whole original IP packet, inner addresses included, and puts it behind a new IP header. Used for site-to-site VPNs.
Integrity check value: the authentication tag at the end of an ESP packet (16 bytes for AES-GCM), or WEP’s encrypted CRC-32.
Initialisation vector: a per-message value fed into a cipher so the same key gives different ciphertext each time. It must not repeat; WEP’s 24-bit IV did.
Filler bytes ESP adds after the payload so the encrypted part ends on a 4-byte boundary (0 to 3 bytes with AES-GCM), followed by a pad-length byte and a next-header byte.
NAT traversal for IPsec (RFC 3948): when IKE detects a NAT, ESP packets are wrapped in UDP port 4500 so NAT devices can track them, adding 8 bytes.
Virtual private cloud: an isolated virtual network in a cloud provider, with its own address range, subnets and routing.

A receiver’s record of recently accepted sequence numbers: packets older than the window or already seen are dropped, while new ones arriving slightly out of order are still accepted. RFC 4303 recommends 64 packets.
An array of bits, one per item, used as a compact set; anti-replay windows commonly use one bit per sequence number.
A fast cryptographic hash function family; WireGuard uses BLAKE2s.
A framework for building Diffie-Hellman-based handshakes from simple patterns; WireGuard’s handshake is built from it.
Replacing session keys with fresh ones after a time or traffic limit, so no key protects too much data or lasts too long.

WireGuard’s rule that each peer’s public key is tied to a list of IP prefixes (AllowedIPs): outgoing packets choose the peer by destination, and decrypted incoming packets must have a source that maps back to the sending peer.
The WireGuard setting listing the IP prefixes a peer may use: it routes matching destinations to that peer and filters the source of packets received from it.
A WireGuard option that sends an authenticated empty packet every N seconds when idle, keeping NAT mappings open.
A VPN set-up that sends only certain destinations (such as internal ranges) through the tunnel, while other traffic goes directly to the internet.
A VPN set-up that sends all traffic through the tunnel, for example with AllowedIPs 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0.
VXLAN tunnel endpoint: the hypervisor or switch that wraps frames into VXLAN and unwraps them.
A switch at the top of each server rack that connects its servers to the data-centre network.
Ethernet VPN (RFC 7432): uses BGP to distribute MAC and IP reachability between tunnel endpoints, reducing reliance on flooding.
Discovering where MAC addresses live by flooding unknown frames everywhere and noting replies, as plain switches and basic VXLAN do.
Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation (RFC 8926, UDP port 6081): an extensible successor to VXLAN with variable-length options.
An AWS service that sends traffic through fleets of virtual appliances such as firewalls, using Geneve encapsulation.
The organised process for handling a security incident: detect, contain, eradicate, recover and learn.
A notice from a vendor describing a vulnerability, affected versions and fixes or mitigations.
The 2004 IEEE amendment that defined robust Wi-Fi security: the four-way handshake, CCMP with AES and 802.1X integration. WPA2 certifies it.
The IEEE amendment adding Protected Management Frames, so robust management frames such as deauthentication can be authenticated.
The IEEE standard for port-based network access control: a device must authenticate (via EAP, usually to a RADIUS server) before its port, wired or wireless, carries normal traffic.
Wi-Fi Protected Access: the 2003 stop-gap that replaced WEP with TKIP so it could run on old hardware. Superseded by WPA2.
The 2004 Wi-Fi security certification based on IEEE 802.11i, using AES-CCMP and the four-way handshake. Personal mode is vulnerable to offline passphrase guessing.
The 2018 Wi-Fi security certification: SAE instead of PSK in Personal mode, mandatory Protected Management Frames, and stronger Enterprise options.
Wi-Fi security where everyone uses one shared passphrase. WPA2-Personal derives keys from it with PSK; WPA3-Personal uses SAE.
Wi-Fi security where each user or device authenticates individually through 802.1X and EAP, usually against a RADIUS server, so each gets its own keys.
A cipher that generates a keystream and XORs it with the data. Reusing a keystream for two messages lets an attacker XOR the ciphertexts and cancel it.
The pseudo-random bit sequence a stream cipher produces from a key and nonce/IV, XORed with plaintext to encrypt it.
The result that among N equally likely values, a repeat becomes likely after only about the square root of N random picks: about 1.18 × √N for a 50 % chance.
example: With 2^24 WEP IVs, about 4,800 frames give a 50 % chance of a repeat.

definition: A 2001 attack exploiting weak RC4 key scheduling when IVs are prepended to the key, which let attackers recover WEP keys from captured traffic.
Pyshkin–Tews–Weinmann (2007): a much faster WEP key-recovery attack that needs only tens of thousands of captured frames.
How a cipher expands its key into internal state. RC4’s was weak, which the FMS and PTW attacks on WEP exploited.

A message authentication code (MAC): a short value computed from a message and a secret key, which only key holders can produce or check. Unlike a checksum such as CRC-32, it cannot be fixed up by an attacker who changes the message.
One secret key used by many devices. If any holder leaks it, or leaves, everyone’s key must change.
Temporal Key Integrity Protocol: WPA’s RC4-based stop-gap that ran on WEP hardware. Deprecated.
Counter Mode CBC-MAC Protocol: WPA2’s AES-based authenticated encryption for data frames. Each frame’s nonce includes a packet number that must never repeat under one key.
Galois/Counter Mode Protocol: an AES-GCM-based Wi-Fi data protection used in newer standards and WPA3 192-bit mode. Nonce reuse lets attackers forge frames.
The human-chosen secret for a WPA2/WPA3-Personal network: 8 to 63 printable ASCII characters. In WPA2 its strength is all that resists offline guessing.
Pairwise Master Key: the 256-bit key from which WPA2/WPA3 session keys are derived. In Personal mode it comes from the passphrase and SSID; in Enterprise mode from 802.1X.

Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 (RFC 8018): turns a password into a key by running a keyed hash many times with a salt, so each guess is expensive. WPA2 uses 4,096 iterations with the SSID as salt.
Deliberately making key derivation from a password slow, by repeating a hash many times, so that every guess costs an attacker the same work.
HMAC built on the SHA-1 hash function; HMAC-SHA1-128 keeps only the first 128 bits. Used in WPA2 key derivation.
Service set identifier: a Wi-Fi network’s name, up to 32 bytes, broadcast by access points. WPA2-Personal uses it as the PBKDF2 salt.
The four EAPOL-Key messages (M1–M4) between access point and client that prove both know the PMK, derive a fresh PTK from nonces and addresses, and deliver the GTK.
The four messages of the WPA2 four-way handshake: M1 carries the AP’s ANonce, M2 the client’s SNonce and a MIC, M3 the encrypted GTK and a MIC, and M4 the client’s acknowledgement.
In 802.1X and WPA2, the device controlling access, usually the access point or switch, which relays authentication and runs the four-way handshake.
In 802.1X and WPA2, the client device or software asking to join, such as wpa_supplicant on Linux.
Pairwise Transient Key: the per-session key set derived in the four-way handshake from the PMK, two nonces and two MAC addresses; it protects unicast traffic between one client and the AP.
Group Temporal Key: the key shared by all clients of an access point for broadcast and multicast frames, delivered encrypted in handshake message 3.
The random nonces in the WPA2 handshake: ANonce from the authenticator (AP) in M1 and SNonce from the supplicant (client) in M2. Both feed the PTK derivation.
Message integrity code: Wi-Fi’s name for a message authentication code. The MIC on handshake messages proves knowledge of the key, and lets an attacker test passphrase guesses offline.
Pseudo-random function: a keyed function whose output looks random to anyone without the key; used to expand a master key into session keys.
Testing password guesses against captured data on the attacker’s own hardware, with no further contact with the target, so there is no lockout or rate limit.
example: Recomputing the MIC from a captured WPA2 handshake for each word in a list.

definition: Guessing passwords from a list of likely choices (words, leaked passwords and variants) rather than every possible string.
Blocking further attempts after too many failed guesses. It only works against online guessing, not offline attacks.

PMK identifier: a 128-bit HMAC-SHA1 value of the PMK, a fixed label and both MAC addresses that some APs send in handshake message 1; it gives attackers an offline verifier without a client handshake.
A measure, in bits, of how many equally likely choices a password could have been: N bits means 2^N possibilities. Only uniform random choices achieve their full entropy.
Key Reinstallation Attacks (Vanhoef, 2017): forcing a WPA2 client to reinstall an in-use key by replaying handshake message 3, which resets its packet number and causes nonce reuse.
Installing a key that is already in use again, which in KRACK resets the nonce counter and so reuses keystream.
The per-frame counter WPA2 includes in each CCMP nonce. It must only increase under one key; KRACK reset it.
The standard open-source Wi-Fi client software on Linux and Android. Unpatched versions 2.4 and later (including 2.6) installed an all-zero key under KRACK.
Google’s Linux-based mobile operating system. Android 6.0 and later used an affected wpa_supplicant and were hit worst by KRACK.
A key of only zero bits, which some wpa_supplicant versions installed after a KRACK reinstall, making traffic trivially decryptable.
IEEE 802.11r: a faster handshake for roaming between access points. Vulnerable AP-side implementations were affected by KRACK.
Basic service set: one access point and the clients associated with it.
A mathematical proof that a protocol meets its security goals under a stated model. KRACK showed the model can miss real-world state machines.

Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: WPA3-Personal’s password-authenticated key exchange, based on Dragonfly. Each guess needs a live exchange, so captured traffic does not allow offline guessing, and it gives forward secrecy.
A password-authenticated key exchange (RFC 7664) on which SAE is based.
Protected Management Frames (802.11w): authenticate robust management frames such as deauthentication after a key is in place, stopping forged kick-offs. Mandatory in WPA3.
Wi-Fi frames that control the connection rather than carry data, such as beacons, association and deauthentication.
A management frame telling a client it is disconnected. Without PMF anyone can forge one, to kick clients off and capture their reconnect handshake.
Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (RFC 8110), certified as Wi-Fi Enhanced Open: encrypts open networks with an unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange. Stops passive sniffing, not evil twins.
Vulnerabilities in WPA3’s SAE found by Vanhoef and Ronen (2019): timing and cache side channels in implementations, and downgrades via transition mode.
An access point setting that accepts both WPA2 and WPA3 clients with the same passphrase, so older devices can join. It allows downgrade to a crackable WPA2 handshake.
A method for SAE to turn the password into an elliptic-curve point in constant time, added to fix Dragonblood timing side channels.
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service: the usual AAA protocol and server behind 802.1X, which checks credentials, sends keying material to the authenticator and can assign a VLAN.
Authentication, authorisation and accounting: the functions of a network access server such as RADIUS: who are you, what may you do, and recording what you did.
Extensible Authentication Protocol: a framework that carries many authentication methods between a client and an authentication server, relayed by the access point.
A specific authentication mechanism carried in EAP, such as EAP-TLS (certificates) or PEAP (password inside TLS). Key-generating methods produce the material for the PMK.
EAP over LAN: the frames that carry EAP and the four-way handshake between client and access point or switch before the port is open.
In 802.1X, the logical port that carries normal traffic only after authentication succeeds; until then only EAPOL passes.
An EAP method where both client and server authenticate with certificates in a TLS handshake. Strong, but needs a client PKI.
Protected EAP: builds a TLS tunnel to the RADIUS server, then runs a password method (usually MSCHAPv2) inside. Safe only if clients verify the server certificate.
EAP Tunneled TLS: like PEAP, a TLS tunnel to the server that protects an inner password exchange.
Microsoft’s challenge–response password protocol. Its DES-based design lets captured exchanges be attacked offline to recover the NT password hash.
Data Encryption Standard: a 1970s block cipher with a 56-bit key, now easily brute-forced; it weakens MSCHAPv2.
Windows’ unsalted MD4 hash of a password. Recovering it from MSCHAPv2 lets an attacker authenticate as the user even without the plaintext password.
Open-source software that turns a Linux machine into a Wi-Fi access point and authenticator; attackers use variants for evil twins.
A worldwide roaming Wi-Fi service for universities and research institutions, using WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X.
IEEE 802.1AE: link-layer encryption and integrity for wired Ethernet between directly connected devices.
Monitoring the radio environment for rogue access points, evil twins, deauthentication floods and other wireless attacks.
Using graphics processors, which run many simple computations in parallel, to test password guesses very quickly.
How long an attacker is inside a network before being detected.
Recording every byte of every packet, usually as pcap files. Detailed but costly: a busy 1 Gbps link fills about 10.8 TB a day, so retention is short or capture is triggered.
Intrusion prevention system: sits inline in the traffic path and can drop malicious traffic, at the cost of latency and a possible point of failure.
Network-based intrusion detection system: an IDS that analyses network traffic, such as Suricata or Zeek at a choke point.
Host-based intrusion detection system: watches activity on one machine, such as processes, files and logs.
Endpoint detection and response: agents on computers that record and analyse process, file and network activity and can contain threats.
Switched Port Analyzer: a switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. An oversubscribed mirror can drop packets.
Test access point: a hardware device inserted in a link that passively copies all its traffic to a monitoring tool.
Cloud equivalent of a SPAN port: copying traffic from virtual network interfaces to monitoring appliances.
Placed directly in the traffic path, so every packet passes through the device, which can therefore block it.
A device that lets traffic through unfiltered when it fails, keeping the network up but unprotected.
A device that blocks all traffic when it fails, staying safe but taking the network down with it.
An alert on benign activity. The false-positive rate is the fraction of benign events wrongly flagged.
An alert on a real attack. The true-positive rate (sensitivity) is the fraction of attacks the detector flags.
The fraction of real attacks a detector flags, also called the true-positive rate or recall.
example: A detector that catches 99 of 100 attacks has 99 % sensitivity.

definition: The fraction of benign events a detector correctly leaves alone: 1 minus the false-positive rate.
The fraction of alerts that are real attacks. With rare attacks it can be tiny even for an accurate detector, which is the base-rate problem.
When attacks are rare (low prevalence, or base rate), even a small false-positive rate produces far more false alerts than true ones. Ignoring this is the base-rate fallacy.
Quickly sorting alerts to decide which need investigation first.
Detection that matches traffic against patterns of known attacks, such as Snort or Suricata rules. Precise for what it describes, but blind to unknown patterns.
Detection that learns a baseline of normal behaviour and alerts on deviations. It can catch new attacks but also flags legitimate changes.
An open-source network intrusion detection and prevention engine using signature rules.
An open-source, multi-threaded IDS/IPS engine that uses Snort-style signature rules and protocol parsers.
An open-source network monitor (formerly Bro) that turns traffic into structured logs, such as conn.log and dns.log, rather than mainly raising signature alerts.
Server Message Block: Windows file-sharing protocol on TCP port 445. A workstation suddenly using it to reach many others suggests lateral movement.
Security information and event management: a system that collects logs from many sources, correlates them and raises alerts.
A decoy system with no legitimate users, so any contact with it is suspicious.
A command-line packet capture and display tool built on libpcap, using BPF capture filters.
The packet capture library under tcpdump and many other tools; it defines the pcap file format.

A capture filter written in the Berkeley Packet Filter language, used by tcpdump and Wireshark’s capture box (for example tcp port 443). On supported live captures it runs in the kernel, discarding unwanted packets early.
How many bytes of each packet a capture keeps; set with tcpdump -s. Truncating saves space but loses payload.
A fixed set of capture files reused in rotation, so a capture can run continuously while keeping only the most recent data.
A network-card mode that passes every frame it sees to the operating system, not just frames addressed to it.
Turning names into addresses (or addresses into names) via DNS or local files. tcpdump -nn turns it off.
A graphical packet analyser that decodes hundreds of protocols and supports display filters and stream reassembly.
Wireshark’s filter language for choosing which captured packets to show, based on decoded fields (tcp.port == 80). Different syntax from BPF capture filters.
The part of Wireshark that decodes one protocol into named fields.
The DNS response code (rcode 3) meaning the name does not exist.
Malware code that generates many pseudo-random domain names to find its command server, causing bursts of NXDOMAIN answers.
An environment variable that makes browsers and many TLS libraries write session secrets to a file, which Wireshark can use to decrypt your own captures.
A named setting passed to programs by the operating system or shell.
Combining several received packets into one large buffer before handing it to the operating system, so captures can show packets bigger than the MTU.
Malware contacting its command server at regular intervals; the timing pattern is visible even when traffic is encrypted.
A short hash or string summarising ClientHello features (versions, cipher suites, extensions), such as JA3 or JA4, used to group similar clients. It is not an authenticated identity.
Records of the names clients looked up through a resolver. Useful for spotting malware domains, but blind to cached answers and to DNS that bypasses the resolver.
A summary of packets sharing selected attributes, typically the 5-tuple, over an interval: timestamps, packet and byte counts and TCP flags, but not payload.
Cisco’s flow-record export protocol (v5, v9), the basis of the IETF’s IPFIX.
IP Flow Information Export (RFC 7011): the IETF standard for exporting flow records from routers or probes to a collector.
A monitoring standard that randomly samples packets (exporting their headers) and interface counters, rather than tracking every flow.
Inspecting only a fraction of packets, such as an average of 1 in 1,000, to cut monitoring cost at the price of missing short flows and adding uncertainty.
The server that receives and stores flow records exported by routers or probes.
AWS’s flow records for traffic on VPC network interfaces: addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, times and ACCEPT/REJECT, aggregated over up to 10 minutes. No payload.
The VPC Flow Logs field saying whether security groups and network ACLs permitted (ACCEPT) or blocked (REJECT) the recorded traffic. It does not name the rule.
The AWS DNS resolver that answers instances’ queries inside a VPC. Its traffic is not in VPC Flow Logs, so Resolver query logs are needed to see DNS activity.
The local AWS endpoint (169.254.169.254) an instance queries for its own configuration and credentials. Its traffic is not in flow logs.
AWS’s hardware and hypervisor platform for modern EC2 instances. Flow logs on Nitro interfaces aggregate over at most one minute.
A VPC Flow Logs status meaning some records were skipped in that interval, for example because of capacity limits or an internal error.
A timestamp counted in seconds since 00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970.
Probing many ports on a host (vertical) or one port across many hosts (horizontal) to find services. Many rejected connections from one source is a classic sign.
The CA that signed a certificate. A client must find the issuer’s certificate to verify the signature and continue up the chain.

Encrypting two messages with the same key and nonce (or IV). For stream ciphers and CTR-based modes such as CCMP and GCM this repeats the keystream, so XORing the ciphertexts reveals the XOR of the plaintexts.
A code-hosting service. In February 2018 it absorbed a 1.35 Tbps memcached amplification attack, then one of the largest reported.
Installing a key that is already in use again. In KRACK this resets the packet number, so nonces and keystream are reused.
A Windows server that runs Active Directory and authenticates users and computers on a corporate network; a prime target for attackers moving laterally.
TLS 1.3’s option to make its handshake look like a resumed TLS 1.2 session, with dummy ChangeCipherSpec messages and a legacy session ID, so that middleboxes do not drop it.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original number: the square root of 16,777,216 is 4,096. Written √.
The full name of TLS: the protocol that encrypts and authenticates connections for HTTPS, email, VPNs and more.

The unit a Wi-Fi link sends: data frames carry packets, management frames control associations, and control frames manage the radio. WPA2/WPA3 encrypt the payload of protected data frames, not their headers.
The readable data before encryption, or after decryption. Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext with a key.
example: In WEP, XORing two ciphertexts made with the same keystream gives the XOR of their two plaintexts.

definition: The scrambled output of encryption. Without the key it should reveal nothing about the plaintext except, usually, its length.

The step in which a Wi-Fi client joins a particular access point, after which the AP accepts its frames. In WPA2/WPA3 the four-way handshake runs after association; frames sent before it (pre-association) are unprotected.
A table of password guesses and the keys or hashes they produce, built in advance so cracking later needs only a lookup. A salt such as the WPA2 SSID means a table works only for that exact salt.
example: A table built for the SSID "linksys" works against every network called linksys, but not against one called "linksys2".

definition: A part of a network separated from the rest, such as one VLAN, subnet or VXLAN network, so traffic between segments can be controlled. In this sense it has nothing to do with a TCP segment.
example: A 12-bit VLAN ID can name 4,094 usable segments; a 24-bit VXLAN VNI about 16.8 million.
